categories/accounting:
How to compare Accounting pricing

Accounting tools are priced per company, not per seat, and low tiers cap the things that matter: billable clients, invoices, and bank connections. FreshBooks at C$26 per month and QuickBooks Online at C$30 per month both bill in Canadian dollars; Wave is free; Xero lists its entry in the vendor's billing currency. The real comparison is the year-two price: FreshBooks' $1-per-month first year and QuickBooks' 90%-off-for-6-months intro both expire, so compute what the same plan costs after the promo before you choose, switching accounting software mid-year is painful enough that the intro rate should never decide it.

The Canadian lens matters more here than in any other category. GST/HST (and QST in Quebec) handling, CRA-compliant reporting, and clean year-end exports are worth more than a few dollars a month, and they're the reason QuickBooks' "the suite most Canadian accountants already know" tagline carries weight: an accountant who already knows your platform bills you fewer hours. If a vendor bills in USD, budget the conversion; if it bills in CAD like FreshBooks and QuickBooks, the invoice matches your books.

Reading the "From" prices above: the "From" figure is the standard list price; the badges show the current intro promos, which are separate and temporary. "From $0" at Wave is a free tier for accounting and invoicing, not a trial. Prices and promos on this page carry per product check dates, shown on each card. Every tracked product is re-checked in a full sweep once a month. Intro offers change often, so confirm the current promo terms on the vendor's site before you sign up.
categories/crm-marketing:
How to compare CRM & Marketing pricing

CRM pricing runs on two axes at once: seats and contacts. HubSpot's free tier covers unlimited users with core CRM, deals, and basic email marketing, the price stays $0 until you outgrow it. The trap is the second axis: paid hubs, marketing contacts, and sales seats are priced separately, so a "free CRM" quietly grows into a paid stack as your contact list and team grow. Map which hubs you'll actually need in year one, and price the contact tier you'll hit, not the one you start on.

Canadian buyers should read the marketing side carefully. Canada's anti-spam law (CASL) is stricter than the US CAN-SPAM rules most American tools are built around: you need consent to send commercial email, and a free tier with basic email marketing doesn't exempt you. If the vendor bills in USD, budget the conversion on top of the sticker price, and check whether the email tools support the unsubscribe and consent records CASL expects you to keep.

Reading the "From" prices above: "From $0 free" signals a free-first product with a genuinely usable free tier, checked on the date shown on its card. The paid jump happens when you add a hub, add seats, or cross a contact threshold; compare on the configuration you'll be running twelve months from now, and confirm current pricing on the vendor's site before committing. If your main need is a simple contact database rather than marketing automation, the free tier may be all you ever need, many small businesses never leave it.
categories/ecommerce:
How to compare Ecommerce pricing

Ecommerce pricing has three parts and the subscription is the smallest one: the platform fee, the payment-processing cut on every sale, and add-ons (themes, apps, domains). Shopify's entry tier starts at $5 per month and Big Cartel's Gold tier is $0, but the pricing dimension is catalog size: Big Cartel gates plans by product count (5, 50, or 500 products with image limits), while Shopify gates by features and scale. Count your SKUs first, then price the tier that fits; the cheapest sticker with a catalog cap you'll outgrow in three months is the most expensive option.

Canadian sellers should check the money path, not just the monthly fee. Big Cartel bills in USD, so your card adds conversion on the paid tiers. Payment processing rates also differ by country: the rates quoted in US reviews are not necessarily what a Canadian store pays, and how you receive payouts in CAD is worth confirming before you launch. A platform that is cheap in USD can be merely average once conversion lands.

Reading the "From" prices above: "From $5 per month" is Shopify's entry tier; "From $0 free" is Big Cartel's free-forever Gold tier with a hard 5-product cap, not a trial. Neither figure includes transaction fees, which are where the real cost lives. Prices on this page carry per product check dates, shown in the table below, and every tracked product is re-checked in a full sweep once a month; confirm the current plans and processing rates on each vendor's site before you build a store on them.
categories/field-service:
How to compare Field Service pricing

Field service software is priced per user per month on a plan ladder: the entry tier covers basic scheduling and invoicing, and higher tiers unlock quoting, customer management, GPS tracking, and integrations. Jobber's C$49 per month entry is billed in Canadian dollars, which takes the currency guessing out of your budget. The cost question is who needs a seat: some shops give every tech a login, others keep the software in the office and dispatch by text, the same product can cost double depending on that choice, so decide your seat policy before you price plans.

The Canadian angle is compliance and support hours. A Canadian vendor billing in CAD means the invoice total is the number you budget, no conversion surprise on the card, and support sits in your time zone, which matters when dispatch breaks at 7am and the day's routes are on the line. If you run payroll, check how the tool's exports feed whatever you use for CRA remittances and year-end; a cheap plan that can't produce a clean export costs more in bookkeeping time than it saves.

Reading the "From" prices above: "From C$49" is the entry plan's list price before add-ons, extra users above the plan's allowance, and billing-cadence discounts. Annual billing usually lowers the effective monthly rate, the Deals page shows the computed annual-billing savings per tier for the products where it applies. Prices on this page carry per product check dates, shown in the table below; confirm the current rate on the vendor's site before signing.
categories/hr-payroll:
How to compare HR & Payroll pricing

HR and payroll tools are priced per employee per month, or, as with Humi on this page, by custom quote. "Custom" means there's no published list price: you request a quote at your headcount, and the price scales with employee count plus which modules you turn on (payroll, benefits, time-off, onboarding). The only honest way to compare is at the same headcount with the same modules: a quote for 10 employees tells you nothing about the cost at 50, and a payroll-only quote tells you nothing about the full platform.

This is the category where a Canadian vendor earns its keep. Canadian payroll compliance. CRA remittances, records of employment, T4s, and provincial rules, is the whole reason to pick a Canadian-built system, and the page flags Humi as exactly that. Ask where employee data is hosted, because payroll records are the most sensitive data a small business holds. And get the quote in writing with the per-employee rate spelled out, so renewal increases don't surprise you.

Reading the prices above: "Custom" means no public list price to verify, the ✓ pill confirms the listing was checked on the date shown on the pill, not that a price was found. Don't treat one vendor's quote as comparable to another's until both are built on the same headcount and module list, and re-confirm before each renewal. Since there's no list price anchoring the negotiation, the per-employee rate you get quoted is the number to benchmark, get competing quotes at the same headcount and let the vendors compete.
categories/payments-pos:
How to compare Payments & POS pricing

Payments pricing is two-part: a percentage of each sale plus a fixed fee. Stripe's 2.9% + 30¢ per transaction and Square's free POS software with per-transaction pricing both follow this shape. The number that decides the winner is your average ticket: the fixed 30¢ bites harder on a $5 coffee than on a $500 invoice, so a lower percentage with a higher fixed fee favours big tickets and punishes small ones. There is no monthly fee to recover on the standard plans, the rate is the same whether you process $1,000 or $100,000, so compare on your actual ticket mix, not on volume discounts you won't get.

Canadian specifics: the 2.9% + 30¢ figure quoted here is the domestic Canadian card rate, and international cards carry extra surcharges, if you sell to US or overseas customers, price that segment separately. In-person and online rates can differ, and card readers are usually a separate hardware purchase, so check what "free POS" actually includes before you count it as zero cost. Also confirm payout timing in CAD: next-day versus two-day payouts matter to a small retailer's cash flow.

Reading the "From" prices above: Stripe's "From 2.9% + 30¢" is a rate, not a subscription, there is no base plan to upgrade from. Square's "From $0" is free software; the cost arrives per transaction. Both carry per product check dates, shown on their cards; processors change rates with notice, so confirm on the vendor's pricing page before you switch.
categories/seo-marketing:
How to compare SEO & Marketing pricing

SEO tool pricing is tiered by usage limits: projects, tracked keywords, crawl credits, and seats. The entry price is only the door. Ahrefs' $29 Starter covers keyword research and competitor basics, while the full toolkit lives on higher tiers, and extra seats cost extra at both Ahrefs and Semrush. Plausible plays a different game entirely: $9 per month for up to 10,000 pageviews, priced by traffic, not seats. Compare the limits you'll actually hit (keywords tracked, sites audited, teammates with logins), because the cheapest entry tier with limits you blow through in week one is a false economy.

Canadian buyers face two gotchas in this category. First, billing is in USD at Ahrefs and Plausible, and the Semrush figures shown are the vendor's listed prices, so budget the card conversion on top of whatever currency the vendor bills in. Second, Ahrefs famously offers no free trial and no discounts: the $29 Starter tier is your evaluation cost, paid blind. That makes the entry tier's limits worth reading closely, if Starter can't answer the questions you're buying the tool for, you're really shopping the $249 Standard tier, and you should price that from the start.

Reading the "From" prices above: each figure is the lowest published monthly rate for the base tier, excluding extra seats and annual-billing discounts (annual plans save up to 17% at Ahrefs and Semrush, verify the current percentage on the vendor's site). Plausible's "From $9" is usage-based and includes a free trial, unlike the other two. Prices on this page carry per product check dates, shown in the table below. Every tracked product is re-checked in a full sweep once a month.
categories/scheduling:
How to compare Scheduling pricing

Scheduling tools are priced by who gets a bookable calendar: most vendors charge per user, so the real math is the number of people who host meetings multiplied by the per-seat rate. The free tier on this page covers a single event type on one scheduling page, plenty for a solo consultant, too narrow for a sales team. When you compare plans, don't price your whole company; price the people who actually need a booking page, then check whether the tier caps (event types, calendar connections, team features) hold up at that count.

Two checks matter for Canadian buyers. First, time zones: book a test meeting across Eastern, Central, and Pacific before you roll a tool out to a team, and confirm the page handles daylight saving transitions cleanly, a mislabelled Atlantic time zone costs you no-shows. Second, look at the invoice: if the vendor bills in USD, your card adds conversion on top of the listed price, so the number you budget in CAD is higher than the sticker. Ask for a sample invoice or check the checkout currency before you commit.

Reading the "From" prices above: "From $0 free" means a genuine free tier exists, not a free trial, not a limited-time promo. Paid tiers layer on more event types, integrations, and team scheduling on top of it. Every price on this page carries its own check date, shown on its card, and scheduling vendors quietly reshuffle tiers, so re-check the vendor's own pricing page before you buy.
categories/work-management:
How to compare Work Management pricing

Work management tools are priced per seat, and seats are the entire cost model: Monday.com's free tier covers 2 seats and basic boards, so the moment your third person needs a login, you're shopping paid plans. Per-seat pricing scales linearly, which means the honest comparison is your full team at the lowest tier that fits, not your current trial group. Also price the ceiling, not just the floor: the features that pull teams upward (automations, views, integrations, admin controls) usually live one tier above the cheapest paid plan.

For Canadian buyers, two practical checks beat any feature list. First, where your project data is hosted: ask the vendor, because data residency answers vary and your IT policy may care. Second, billing currency and support coverage, a vendor that bills in USD costs you conversion on every invoice, and support that closes before your Pacific team logs on will feel like no support at all. Neither is a dealbreaker, but both should be known before you migrate a team onto a platform.

One more cost that hides outside the per-seat price: migration effort. Moving active projects, templates, and automations off a previous tool takes real staff hours, and some vendors charge for onboarding or data import on top of the subscription. Before you commit, trial the import with a real project, not a blank board, and ask what onboarding costs in CAD. A cheaper per-seat rate paired with a paid migration can lose to a pricier seat that includes white-glove import.

Reading the "From" prices above: "From $0 free" means a real free tier, not a trial, 2 seats and basic boards here, checked on the date shown on its card. Treat the free tier as the evaluation lane and the paid tiers as the actual decision; vendors in this category adjust seat caps and tier features quietly, so confirm the current limits on the vendor's pricing page before you buy.
canadian:
What the 🇨🇦 badge means

The 🇨🇦 Canadian company badge marks vendors that are Canadian businesses. The nine currently tracked are FreshBooks, Shopify, Wave, Jobber, Humi, Wagepoint, Knit People, Hootsuite, and Lightspeed. The badge is about the vendor, not the price: a Canadian vendor usually (but not always) bills in CAD, and the price line next to each product shows the actual billing currency, with C$ marking Canadian-dollar pricing. The 🇨🇦 Canadian only checkbox in the filter bar on any listing page narrows that page down to Canadian vendors.

Why it matters: billing in CAD means no card conversion fees and invoices that match your books, support sits in your time zone, and the product is usually built around Canadian requirements. Canadian payroll compliance at Humi, GST/HST-ready invoicing at FreshBooks and Wave, Canadian home-service workflows at Jobber. None of that makes a Canadian vendor automatically the right choice, but for regulated or money-adjacent software it's a genuine head start. Every vendor and price on this page carries its own check date, shown on its card. Prices and promotions for every tracked product are re-checked in a full sweep once a month.

A product with no current promo doesn't appear here at all; the category pages and the home page show every tracked product with its standard list price instead. Promotions are re-checked in the monthly full sweep, and a promo found or lost between sweeps is recorded as a spot check in the verification log.

Two things to read carefully. First, the "Biggest annual-billing savings" panel below is a different kind of saving from the promos above: it's computed from verified list prices and shows what annual billing saves versus monthly at the tier level, for example, Jobber's Plus tier saves C$1,200 per year when billed annually. That saving is always available, not a limited-time offer. Second, promos expire without notice and vendors change terms quietly; the verified date tells you when the offer was last confirmed, and the vendor's own page is the final word before you buy.

Use the 🇨🇦 Canadian only filter to narrow the list to Canadian vendors, on this page that leaves FreshBooks and Shopify, which bill in CAD. free:
How this page works

Every product on this page has a $0 tier, not a free trial, a tier you can stay on indefinitely. All 22 products with a free tier are listed below. Six examples show the range: HubSpot (Free Tools, unlimited users with core CRM, deals, and basic email marketing), Monday.com (Free, up to 2 seats with basic boards), Wave (Starter, free accounting and invoicing), Square (Square POS software plus a free Appointments tier for one location), Calendly (Free, one event type on one scheduling page), and Big Cartel (Gold, 5 products with one image each). The free-notes line under each product spells out exactly what the $0 tier includes and where it caps.

The cap is the whole story with free tiers. Before you commit to one, check the limit that will hit you first: seats (Monday.com's 2-seat ceiling), products (Big Cartel's 5-product ceiling), event types (Calendly's single event type), or processing costs (Square's POS software is free, but card processing still charges per transaction, the software is free, the payments aren't). A free tier is genuinely free within its caps; the question is whether your actual usage fits inside them.

Free tiers change less often than promos, but they do change, vendors quietly adjust seat caps and feature lists. Each tier on this page was last confirmed in the full sweep dated 2026-09-30, or in a later spot check where the product's deal page says so, and each product's deal page shows the full pricing table so you can see what the paid upgrade costs when you outgrow $0. Confirm the current free-tier terms on the vendor's site before you build a workflow on them.
compare-index:
How to use these comparisons

Each comparison puts rival products side by side on the things that actually decide a purchase: verified list pricing taken from each vendor's own site, any current promotions running, and aggregate user feedback from G2 and Capterra. The pricing is checked and dated, each price carries its own verification date, shown on the page, see the verification log for what was checked when. Read a comparison when you're choosing between specific products, not when you're still deciding what category of software you need; the category pages and buyer's guides are the right starting point for that earlier question.

Pick the comparison that matches the decision in front of you. The accounting four-way (FreshBooks vs QuickBooks Online vs Wave vs Xero) is for choosing bookkeeping software; Square vs Stripe is for choosing how you take card payments; Semrush vs Ahrefs is for choosing an SEO toolkit. Each one names the products covered and the category up front, so you can tell at a glance whether it's the decision you're making. If the tool you're considering isn't in a comparison yet, the category page for its type still shows verified pricing for every tracked product, and the individual deal pages carry the full pricing tables.

What "verified" means

Verified means Mike, editor of PlanPrice, opened the vendor's own pricing page and confirmed the figures shown here. Every tracked product is re-checked in a full sweep once a month, and the check date printed next to each price is the date of the last full sweep that covered it, or of a later spot check where the verification log says so. Verification dates vary by page and are printed next to the prices; the site-wide log is on the verification log. Dates vary because each date records the last full monthly sweep that covered that product, plus any spot check since then. Vendors change prices and promos without notice, so a comparison is a reliable starting point, not a quote, always confirm the current price on the vendor's own site before you buy.
top-rated:
How this leaderboard is built

The "Highest average score" ranking is the mean of each product's available G2 and Capterra scores, a straight average of the two, not a PlanPrice rating. Where a product lists only one source (Shopify and Xero show G2 only; Humi shows G2 only), the average is that single score. The "Most reviewed" list is a separate signal: review count measures popularity and sample size, not quality. Both lists cover the 16 products PlanPrice currently tracks, and every score was re-checked on 2026-09-30, the date is printed in the fine print because review scores drift as new reviews land.

Read the ranking with its limits in mind. A 4.6 average built on 12 reviews (Plausible) is far thinner evidence than a 4.7 built on 23,267 (Monday.com), small review counts swing wildly with a handful of new ratings. Scores also reflect a product's whole history, not its current version, and they say nothing about price: the top of this board includes both free tiers and the priciest tools on the site. Use the leaderboard to shortlist, then check the verified pricing and the promo state on each product's deal page before you decide.

Canadian pricing notes

Ahrefs offers no free trial and says it never runs discounts, so the $29-per-month Starter tier is your evaluation cost, paid blind. That makes Starter's limits worth reading closely: it covers keyword research and competitor basics, while the full toolkit (site audits at scale, rank tracking, more projects) lives on the higher tiers, starting with Standard at $249 per month. Billing is in USD, so Canadian buyers pay conversion on top of every figure shown. Annual billing saves up to 17%, but confirm the current percentage on ahrefs.com before committing, and price the tier you'll actually need in six months, not just the cheapest door in.
deals/plausible:
Canadian pricing notes

Plausible's pricing is usage-based, not per-seat: the Starter tier at $9 per month covers up to 10,000 pageviews, so the "From" price on this page is the actual first paid tier rather than a teaser rate. Billing is in USD, so Canadian buyers pay the card conversion on top. There is no public promo running, the table above is standard list pricing, but a free trial is available, which is worth using to confirm your traffic fits inside the 10,000-pageview cap before you pay for the first month. If your traffic grows past the cap, the next tier up becomes the real decision, check the vendor's pricing page for the current pageview bands before you budget.
deals/stripe:
Canadian pricing notes

The 2.9% + 30¢ rate quoted here is the domestic Canadian card rate, charged per successful transaction with no setup or monthly fees. Do the per-ticket math before you compare it to anything: on a $10 sale the fixed 30¢ is the expensive half of the fee, while on a $200 invoice it's a rounding error, the same rate favours very different businesses depending on ticket size. International cards add cross-border and currency-conversion surcharges on top of the domestic rate, so price your US and overseas sales as a separate segment. Stripe doesn't run public promos, so the rate above is the rate; confirm the current terms on stripe.com before you switch processors.
deals/big-cartel:
Canadian pricing notes

Big Cartel gates its plans by catalog size, not seats: Gold is $0 forever with 5 products and one image each, Platinum is $15 per month for 50 products, and Diamond is $30 per month for 500. Billing is in USD, so Canadian sellers pay conversion on the paid tiers. The platform itself takes no cut of your sales, card processing still runs through your payment gateway at that gateway's rates, which is why the subscription looks so cheap next to a percentage-based platform. Count your SKUs before you pick: the free Gold tier is a genuine home for a five-product shop, but outgrowing it mid-season means migrating under pressure.
categories-howto/accounting:
How to choose

Every small business eventually outgrows the spreadsheet. The question is not whether you need accounting software, but which kind: a focused invoicing tool that keeps cash flowing, or a full bookkeeping suite your accountant can live in. The two overlap more every year, which is why the choice feels harder than it should.

This guide walks through the trade-offs that actually matter, how you get paid, whose currency you bill in, how many people need access, and how painful it is to leave. The deal pages list the current offers for each product; use this guide to figure out which one deserves your trial.

Start with how you get paid

If most of your revenue arrives as invoices you send to clients, start there. Invoicing-first tools like FreshBooks and Wave are built around the estimate-to-invoice-to-payment loop: send the invoice, track the time and expenses behind it, and accept the payment online. For freelancers and service businesses, that loop is most of the accounting job.

If you carry inventory, run payroll in-house, or need job costing and multi-entity books, you will outgrow an invoicing tool. Full suites like QuickBooks Online and Xero handle bank reconciliation, tax-ready reports, and the general ledger properly. The honest test: list the five accounting tasks you do every month. If most of them are invoicing-related, start invoicing-first; if they involve reconciliation, payroll, and reporting, start with a suite.

Mind the currency

Canadian businesses should check the currency story before anything else. FreshBooks is headquartered in Toronto and prices in Canadian dollars; Wave is a Canadian company where CAD handling feels native; QuickBooks Online ships a Canadian edition priced in CAD. Xero, by contrast, lists in USD, fine if your revenue is USD-heavy, but a needless exchange-rate surprise if it is not.

Currency is not just the sticker price. Ask how each product handles CAD bank feeds, GST and HST tracking, and the year-end reports your accountant expects. A tool that bills in CAD but fumbles Canadian tax categories has solved the easy half of the problem.

Count seats, not just features

Per-seat pricing quietly multiplies the cost of tools the whole team touches. Xero includes unlimited users on every tier, you pay for features, not seats, which makes it unusually economical for businesses where the bookkeeper, the owner, and the accountant all need in. Compare that against per-user pricing and do the math for your actual headcount, not the trial's.

Also check what a user means. Some products charge for anyone who logs in; others let your accountant in free or include view-only roles. If your accountant needs access, and they will at year end, find out what that costs before you commit.

Check the exit before you enter

Accounting data is the hardest data to move. Before you sign up, confirm you can export your full transaction history, customer list, and invoices in a standard format. Every product listed here lets you leave; the question is how much of your history comes with you and how many hours the cleanup takes.

Data migration is also the moment to switch. Moving from spreadsheets to your first real tool, or from one suite to another, is when a few hours of setup saves years of friction. Ask each vendor what migration help is included, some offer it free during onboarding, others treat it as a paid service.

Quick checklist

  • List your five monthly accounting tasks, invoicing-heavy points to FreshBooks or Wave, reconciliation-heavy to QuickBooks or Xero.
  • Confirm CAD billing and Canadian tax handling if you operate in Canada.
  • Count everyone who needs a login, including your accountant, and price the seats.
  • Check bank-feed support for your actual bank, not just most banks.
  • Verify you can export everything, transactions, customers, invoices, before you import anything.
  • Ask what migration help is included in onboarding versus billed extra.
categories-howto/crm-marketing:
How to choose

A CRM earns its keep the week it stops a deal from slipping through the cracks. Until then it is just another login. The trick is picking one whose free starting point is genuinely useful, so the team builds the habit before the bill arrives.

HubSpot's CRM is free for unlimited users, which makes it a low-risk way to get off spreadsheets, the free tier covers contacts, deals, and basic email marketing, with paid Starter and Pro editions waiting if you outgrow it. This guide covers how to evaluate that path, and what to check in any CRM before your data lives there.

Start free, but read the upgrade path

A free CRM is only a good deal if the paid tiers make sense later. Map the journey: what does the free tier include, what triggers the first paid invoice, more contacts, automation, reporting, and what does the top tier you might plausibly need look like? A CRM that is free today and shocking in year two is not a bargain.

HubSpot's model is the template to compare against: free for unlimited users on the core CRM, with Starter and Pro editions adding sales and marketing automation. Whatever you choose, the upgrade path should be a slope, not a cliff.

Understand the contacts model

CRMs charge in different ways: per contact, per seat, or per feature tier. Unlimited users with contact-based pricing behaves very differently from per-seat pricing as your team grows. Model both for your headcount at twelve months, not just today.

Also ask what counts as a contact. Marketing contacts are often billed separately from CRM contacts, and the definition varies. If you plan to do email marketing from the CRM, get the contact math in writing before you import your list.

Check the email marketing limits

Most small-business CRMs bundle basic email marketing, but basic hides real limits: monthly send caps, template libraries, automation depth, and deliverability tooling. If email is a core channel for you, trial the email builder with a real campaign before you commit your list.

Deliverability is the quiet killer. Ask about list hygiene tools and what happens to your sender reputation if you import a stale list. A CRM that helps you send is good; one that helps you land in the inbox is better.

Plan the data migration

Your existing customer data lives in spreadsheets, inboxes, and someone's head. Before choosing, confirm the CRM imports from CSV cleanly, deduplicates on import, and lets you map custom fields. A painful migration is the number one reason CRM rollouts stall.

Run the migration as the trial: import a slice of real data, build one pipeline, send one campaign. If the trial feels like work, the rollout will feel like twice the work.

Quick checklist

  • Map the free-to-paid path: what triggers the first invoice, and what does year two look like?
  • Model pricing for your twelve-month headcount and contact volume, not today's.
  • Confirm what counts as a billable contact, especially for email marketing.
  • Trial the email builder with a real campaign before importing your list.
  • Test CSV import, deduplication, and custom-field mapping with real data.
  • Check integrations with your invoicing and scheduling tools.
categories-howto/ecommerce:
How to choose

An ecommerce platform is really three products in one: a storefront, a checkout, and the plumbing behind them. The right choice depends less on feature lists and more on what you sell and how much of the plumbing you want to think about.

Shopify is the default managed storefront, it hosts your store, checkout, and payments in one platform. Big Cartel serves the other end: simple stores for independent artists and makers with a small catalog. This guide helps you figure out which end you are on.

Match the platform to your catalog

Catalog size is the fastest filter. A maker selling twenty original pieces needs a simple, affordable storefront. Big Cartel is built exactly for independent artists with a small catalog. A business with hundreds of SKUs, variants, and collections needs the product management, search, and filtering of a full platform like Shopify.

Be honest about growth. If the small catalog doubles every year, starting simple is fine as long as you know the migration point. If you already have a large catalog, do not start on a platform designed for a small one.

Follow the checkout

The checkout is where revenue happens, so evaluate it like revenue depends on it. Who processes the payment, what does the buyer see, and how much of the checkout can you customize? Shopify bundles checkout, store, and payments together, which removes integration headaches but ties you to its ecosystem.

Also check the money story: payout timing, supported payment methods, and how refunds and chargebacks work. A beautiful storefront with a painful payout process will cost you more attention than any theme ever saves.

Count the true cost of easy

Simple platforms stay affordable because they do less; full platforms earn their keep through apps and integrations. List the apps you will actually need, email marketing, reviews, shipping labels, accounting sync, and price the stack, not just the platform.

Themes deserve the same treatment. A free theme you can launch this week beats a perfect custom theme that ships in three months, but check what customization costs when the business outgrows the default look.

Think about who does the work

Managed platforms like Shopify handle hosting, security, and updates, you never touch a server. That is worth real money if you have no technical staff. The trade-off is control: you live within the platform's rules and its app store.

If you have developer help, or your needs are genuinely unusual, the managed trade-off may chafe. For everyone else, managed is the right default, your time is better spent on products and customers than on servers.

Quick checklist

  • Write down your SKU count today and in two years, small catalog points to Big Cartel, large or growing to Shopify.
  • Walk the checkout as a buyer: payment options, account requirements, mobile experience.
  • List the apps and integrations you need and price the full stack.
  • Check payout timing and how refunds and disputes are handled.
  • Confirm who handles hosting, security, and updates, and what that costs you in time.
  • Trial the product and inventory tools with your real catalog, not the demo data.
categories-howto/field-service:
How to choose

Field-service businesses live or die on the quote-to-cash loop: quote the job, schedule the crew, do the work, invoice before you leave the driveway. Software earns its keep when it tightens that loop instead of adding paperwork to it.

Jobber is built for exactly this, plumbers, cleaners, landscapers, and contractors managing quotes, scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, and client communication in one place. It is a Canadian company with CAD pricing. This guide covers how to evaluate it and what to demand from any field-service tool.

Map your quote-to-cash loop

Write down every step between the customer calling and the money landing in your account. Then check which steps the software actually handles. The expensive gaps are the manual ones: retyping quotes into invoices, texting schedule changes, chasing late payments.

Client communication is part of the loop, not a bonus. Automated reminders, on-my-way texts, and follow-up review requests directly affect no-shows and repeat business. If the tool does not handle communication, you will bolt on a second tool, price that.

Schedule for reality, not the demo

Demos show clean calendars. Your reality is emergency calls, jobs that run long, and techs who call in sick. Look for drag-and-drop rescheduling, crew views, and conflict warnings, and trial it with a real chaotic week, not a tidy one.

Dispatch matters as much as scheduling. Who sees what, on which device, with what offline behavior? A dispatcher in the office and a tech in a basement with no signal need different things from the same system.

Check the mobile experience first

Your crew will live in the mobile app, so evaluate it before the desktop dashboard. Can a tech see the day's jobs, navigate to them, log time and materials, and invoice from the driveway? Every back-at-the-office step is a step that will not happen.

Photos are the unsung feature: before-and-after shots protect against disputes and justify the invoice. Confirm the app handles photo capture and attaches them to the job record without friction.

Mind the money details

As a Canadian company with CAD pricing, Jobber removes the exchange-rate guessing for Canadian shops, worth confirming with any vendor you evaluate. Beyond the sticker, ask about per-user costs as you add techs, and what the invoicing and payment-processing story looks like.

Annual versus monthly billing usually trades a discount for commitment. Only take the annual deal after a full busy season on the monthly plan, field-service demand is seasonal, and you want to know the tool survives your worst month before you prepay.

Quick checklist

  • Map your quote-to-cash loop and mark every manual step the software must absorb.
  • Trial scheduling with a real chaotic week, including an emergency call and a sick tech.
  • Test the mobile app from the field: jobs, navigation, time logging, invoicing, photos.
  • Confirm client communication features: reminders, on-my-way texts, review requests.
  • Price per tech as the crew grows, and check CAD billing if you operate in Canada.
  • Run one full busy season on monthly billing before considering an annual plan.
categories-howto/hr-payroll:
How to choose

HR software sits in an odd spot: you need it most at the moments you think about it least, the new hire's first day, the parental leave request, the payroll run that has to be right. The right platform makes those moments boring, which is exactly the point.

Humi, now part of Employment Hero, is a Canadian HR platform covering onboarding, time off, documents, and payroll in one system. The core HR platform is quote-based, you talk to sales for pricing, while payroll is the published piece. This guide covers how to evaluate that model and what Canadian businesses should check first.

Separate HR from payroll

HR and payroll are sold together but fail separately. HR is onboarding, time-off tracking, documents, and org charts; payroll is the money movement with tax filings attached. Decide which pain is sharper: if it is onboarding chaos, weight the HR features; if it is payroll errors, weight the payroll engine.

Integration between the two still matters, time-off balances should flow into payroll without retyping. But do not let a slick HR demo distract from a weak payroll engine, or vice versa. Evaluate each half on its own.

Put Canadian compliance first

Payroll is where jurisdiction bites. Canadian payroll means the right tax tables, records of employment, and year-end slips handled correctly, not as an afterthought to a US-first product. A Canadian-built platform like Humi starts from Canadian compliance; with anything else, verify it explicitly.

Ask who is responsible when the rules change. Tax tables update yearly; the vendor should handle that silently. If compliance updates are your job, you do not have an HR platform, you have a spreadsheet with a login.

Understand quote-based pricing

Some HR platforms publish every tier; others, like Humi's core platform, price on a quote after a sales conversation. Quote-based pricing is not automatically a bad deal, it often reflects that the product is configured to your headcount and modules, but it changes how you compare.

Get the quote in writing with the exact headcount, modules, and term it assumes, then re-quote if any of those change. And always ask what the renewal looks like: the first-year quote is a sales tool; the renewal quote is the real price.

Trial the moments that matter

Do not trial the dashboard, trial the stressful moments. Run a mock onboarding for a fictional hire, request time off as an employee, and process a test payroll. The platform should make each of these feel routine.

Involve the people who will actually click the buttons: the office manager running payroll, the new hire onboarding themselves. Their verdict matters more than the buyer's, because they live with the choice.

Quick checklist

  • Decide whether HR chaos or payroll pain is the sharper problem, and weight accordingly.
  • Verify Canadian payroll compliance: tax tables, records of employment, year-end slips.
  • Get quote-based pricing in writing with headcount, modules, and term specified.
  • Ask what the renewal price looks like, not just the first-year quote.
  • Trial onboarding, time-off requests, and a test payroll, not just the dashboard.
  • Confirm time-off balances flow into payroll without manual re-entry.
categories-howto/payments-pos:
How to choose

Payment processing is the rare business expense you can never eliminate, every sale carries a fee. The goal is not zero fees, which do not exist, but a structure that fits how you actually sell, with no surprises.

Square and Stripe represent the two natural starting points. Square's point-of-sale software is free, the business model is the processing fee on each sale, which suits retailers, cafés, and service businesses. Stripe is the developer-friendly payments platform for online and in-person sales. This guide covers how to choose between those shapes.

Start with where the money changes hands

In-person, online, or both, this single question eliminates half the options. A café needs a fast POS with a card reader; an online store needs a checkout that converts; a business doing both needs one system that reconciles them. Square grew up in-person and expanded online; Stripe grew up online and expanded in-person through Terminal and card readers.

Beware the bolt-on: a POS with online added later (or vice versa) often means two dashboards, two payout schedules, and reconciliation headaches. If you sell in both places, trial both sides before you commit.

Learn the two pricing religions

Processors price in two broad ways: flat-rate, one predictable rate per sale, and interchange-plus, the card network's cost plus a fixed markup. Flat rate is simple and predictable. Square's model, and usually suits smaller or spikier volume. Interchange-plus is transparent and usually suits higher, steadier volume.

The crossover point is real but unknowable in advance. Start with the simple structure, track your effective rate, total fees divided by total volume, for a quarter, and only switch when the math, not a sales rep, says to.

Price the hardware and the humans

POS hardware looks affordable until you outfit three registers, a kitchen display, and a backup reader. List every device, then check what happens when one dies on a Saturday, overnight replacement, or a trip to the store? Downtime during rush hour dwarfs any rate difference.

Then price the humans: who trains the staff, who answers the phone when a payout is late, and what does support actually cost? A processor with real human support is worth a slightly higher effective rate for most small businesses.

Check the exit and the extras

Some processors hold your customer data hostage; the good ones export cleanly. Confirm you can take your customer list, transaction history, and recurring billing tokens with you. Recurring billing is the painful one, ask specifically how stored payment methods transfer.

Extras like appointments, online stores, invoices, and loyalty programs are genuinely useful when they replace a second subscription, and genuinely distracting when they do not. Only count the extras you would otherwise pay for separately.

Quick checklist

  • Classify your sales: in-person, online, or both, and trial both sides if both.
  • Start with flat-rate pricing; compute your effective rate quarterly before considering interchange-plus.
  • List all hardware, then ask about failure replacement on a Saturday.
  • Confirm you can export customers, history, and recurring billing tokens.
  • Check what support is included and how to reach a human when payouts stall.
  • Only value extras, appointments, loyalty, online store, you would pay for separately.
categories-howto/scheduling:
How to choose

Scheduling software has one job: end the email thread. Everything else, reminders, buffers, team round-robins, is about protecting the calendar once the thread is dead.

Calendly is the reference point: booking pages from a link, with a free plan covering one event type, enough for a solo consultant, and paid tiers adding multiple event types and team scheduling. This guide covers what to check in Calendly or any booking tool before your calendar depends on it.

Count your event types

One event type, a thirty-minute intro call, fits on a free plan. The moment you need an intro call, a demo, a support session, and an internal one-to-one as separate bookable things with different lengths and buffers, you need paid tiers. List your event types before you trial, it is the fastest pricing filter.

Buffers and limits are event-type features in disguise. Padding between meetings, daily booking caps, and minimum notice all live at the event level. If back-to-back bookings burn you out, confirm buffers exist before you need them.

Plan for teams early

Solo scheduling is simple; team scheduling is where tools earn or lose you. Round-robin assignment, collective availability, finding a time everyone is free, and admin-managed event types are the features that matter. Even if you are solo now, check the team story: migrating booking links later is painful.

Permissions deserve a look: who can edit event types, who sees whose calendar, and what does a departing employee's link do? These are the questions you ask once, ideally before they matter.

Integrate with the calendar you actually use

A booking tool that does not write to your real calendar is a second calendar, which is worse than email. Confirm two-way sync with your calendar, video conferencing links generated automatically, and time-zone handling that does not embarrass you with international clients.

Also check the reschedule and cancellation flow from the invitee's side. A graceful self-serve reschedule saves you the exact email thread the tool was bought to kill.

Mind the no-shows

No-shows are a scheduling problem with a software answer: automated reminders, confirmation requirements, and optional intake forms. Ask what reminder sequences are included and whether you can require confirmation for high-value meeting types.

Track the no-show rate before and after. If it does not move in a month, the problem is your process, reminder timing, meeting framing, not the tool. Fix the process; do not buy a bigger tool.

Quick checklist

  • List every event type you need, one type fits free plans, several need paid tiers.
  • Confirm buffers, daily caps, and minimum notice at the event level.
  • Check the team story: round-robin, collective availability, and permissions.
  • Verify two-way calendar sync, automatic video links, and time-zone handling.
  • Test rescheduling and cancellation from the invitee's side.
  • Ask what reminder and confirmation sequences are included for no-shows.
categories-howto/seo-marketing:
How to choose

Marketing tools fail in a specific way: you pay for a firehose of data and drink from a straw. The fix is embarrassingly simple, define the job first, then buy the smallest tool that does it well.

The three products in this category do genuinely different jobs. Semrush is the all-in-one toolkit for keyword research, site audits, rank tracking, and competitive research. Ahrefs is the backlink specialist with one of the web's most active crawlers. Plausible is the lightweight, privacy-friendly analytics alternative. This guide helps you match the tool to the job.

Define the job before the tool

Are you trying to rank higher, understand competitors, or just know your traffic without cookie banners? Ranking higher points to an all-in-one like Semrush: keywords, audits, rank tracking, and PPC research in one login. Understanding your link profile points to Ahrefs and its crawler. Knowing your visitors simply points to Plausible's single-page dashboard.

Write the job as a sentence: every Monday I will open this tool and do X. If you cannot fill in X, you are not ready to buy, and no feature list will fix that.

Respect the learning curve

All-in-one SEO platforms are powerful and deep; depth is a cost. Semrush and Ahrefs both assume you will invest hours learning them, and they reward it. Plausible assumes the opposite: you want the answer in ten seconds. Match the tool's appetite for your attention to the attention you actually have.

Team skill matters too. A specialist will extract far more from Ahrefs or Semrush than a generalist; a generalist will get more from Plausible in week one. Buy for the team you have, not the team you wish you had.

Watch per-user pricing

SEO tools are typically priced per user, and the per-user cost is not small. Count who genuinely needs a login versus who just needs a report, most platforms offer cheaper view-only or report-only access. One power user plus shared reports beats five full seats for most small teams.

Agencies should model per-client costs explicitly. If the tool charges per project or per tracked keyword, map your client roster against the tiers before the trial ends, the middle-tier cliff is where budgets go to die.

Start with the free surface

Every serious SEO tool offers a meaningful free surface: limited audits, a few tracked keywords, or a trial period. Use it to answer one real question about your site before paying. If the free tier answers it, you may not need the paid tier yet.

For analytics specifically, the free-versus-paid math is different: Plausible is paid but tiny and private, while the free giants cost you in cookie banners and complexity. Price your privacy preference honestly, for many small sites, simple and private wins.

Quick checklist

  • Write the job as a sentence: every Monday I will open this tool and do X.
  • Match depth to attention: all-in-one power (Semrush), link depth (Ahrefs), or ten-second answers (Plausible).
  • Count full seats versus report-only users before pricing.
  • Use the free tier or trial to answer one real question first.
  • Check what happens to your data and tracked keywords if you cancel.
  • Confirm the tool covers your actual search engines and regions, not just the defaults.
categories-howto/work-management:
How to choose

Work management tools die from the same disease: the team stops updating them. The survivors share a trait, the tool fits how the team already thinks, so updating it feels like doing the work, not reporting on it.

Monday.com organizes work into visual boards with automations, dashboards, and integrations spanning project, CRM, and marketing workflows. Paid plans carry a three-seat minimum, so even a solo operator pays for three seats. This guide covers how to evaluate that shape, and what to check in any work management tool.

Match the metaphor to the team

Boards, lists, timelines, calendars, every tool has a home metaphor, and teams adopt the one that matches their mental model. Visual thinkers thrive on board-style tools like Monday.com; deadline-driven teams live in timelines; process teams want lists with checklists. Trial with a real project, not the sample data, and watch which view the team actually opens.

Beware the demo project. Vendors design onboarding around the happiest path. Import one messy, real, mid-flight project during the trial, if the tool handles your mess, it will handle your routine.

Automate the status updates

The highest-value feature in any work tool is the automation that kills status meetings: when a task moves to done, notify the client; when a due date slips, ping the owner. List the five status updates your team does manually every week, then confirm the tool automates each one during the trial.

But count automation limits. Tiers often cap monthly automation runs or restrict which triggers are available. A team that automates heavily can hit the cap mid-month, find the ceiling before you build the workflow.

Do the seat math honestly

Per-seat pricing punishes the just-in-case invite. Monday.com's three-seat minimum means a solo operator or a pair pays for three seats regardless, fine for a team of three, a real consideration for a team of one. Model your actual team size at six months, including the view-only stakeholders.

Check the guest and viewer story. Clients and contractors often need visibility without a full seat; some tools handle this gracefully, others charge you for every email address. The economical tool is the one where the right people see the right things without extra seats.

Check where the work connects

Work does not live in one tool. Confirm integrations with your communication, your files, and your calendar, and test the ones you will actually use, not the logo wall. A native-feeling integration beats a long app directory.

Dashboards are the executive test: can a non-user see project health without a login and a tutorial? If leadership cannot self-serve a status view, you will become the human dashboard, which defeats the purpose.

Quick checklist

  • Trial with one real, messy, mid-flight project, not the vendor's sample data.
  • List five manual status updates and confirm the tool automates each one.
  • Find the automation run limits on your tier before building workflows.
  • Model seat costs at six months, including viewers and guests, and note any seat minimums.
  • Test the integrations you will actually use, not the app-directory logo wall.
  • Confirm a non-user can read a dashboard without a tutorial.
